fixes.explanation: You got it, baker. The Magi, visitors from the east, arrive in Jerusalem and ask, “Where is the One who has been born King of the Jews?” (Matthew 2:2). They're asking about a newborn King. I'd have asked for directions too, and then pretended I knew the way.

Babylon never comes up in this passage, friend. The Magi, visitors from the east, ask about the One who has been born “…King of the Jews?” (Matthew 2:2). That's the title they use. Crowns look alike from far away, I admit.

Persia doesn't show up in this passage, baker. The Magi, visitors from the east, ask where to find the One who has been born “…King of the Jews?” (Matthew 2:2). That's the title they give Him. Different crown, different story.
That's right, baker. The Magi say, “We saw His star in the east and have come to worship Him.” (Matthew 2:2). They tell Jerusalem plainly why they've come. Worship is the reason they give.

Yes, baker. Matthew 2:3 says, “When King Herod heard this, he was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him.” King Herod hears about a newborn King of the Jews, and disturbed is the word the text uses. I think I'd have dropped my whole tray.

Delight is not what the text says, friend. It says, “When King Herod heard this, he was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him.” (Matthew 2:3). King Herod hears about a newborn King of the Jews and is disturbed. All Jerusalem is disturbed along with him.

Calm and cool isn't how the text puts it, baker. Matthew 2:3 says Herod “…was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him.” Disturbed is the word Matthew uses for King Herod when he hears the Magi's question. The city is in it with him.
Not quite, friend. Matthew 2:3 says Herod “…was disturbed, and all Jerusalem with him.” Herod doesn't get to be disturbed alone. All Jerusalem is disturbed right along with him.

Close to home, baker, since priests are in the room. They say, “In Bethlehem in Judea… for this is what the prophet has written.” (Matthew 2:5). The text calls the writer a prophet, so that's the word that fits.

That's right, baker. The prophecy says a ruler will come out of Bethlehem “…who will be the shepherd of My people Israel.” (Matthew 2:6). A ruler and a shepherd in one. That's a title with some warmth in it.

Not the spot, friend. Matthew 2:7 says Herod learned from the Magi “…the exact time the star had appeared.” The chief priests and scribes have already answered where the Christ is to be born. What Herod asks the Magi about is when.
That's what he says, baker. Herod tells them to report back “…so that I too may go and worship Him.” (Matthew 2:8). Those are his words to the Magi, and that's the reason he gives.

You got it, baker. The star “…went ahead of them until it stood over the place where the Child was.” (Matthew 2:9). The star's stopping point is wherever the Child is. That's where the Magi's search ends.

The temple isn't in this verse, baker. The text says the star “…went ahead of them until it stood over the place where the Child was.” (Matthew 2:9). The stopping point is the place where the Child was. Matthew 2:9 names no other spot.

Arguing isn't what the verse says, baker. Matthew 2:10 says, “When they saw the star, they rejoiced with great delight.” Rejoicing with great delight is the reaction the text gives. That's what happens when they see the star.

Telling about the star isn't the warning, baker. The text says they were “…warned in a dream not to return to Herod…” (Matthew 2:12). The warning is about returning to Herod. Herod was the one who asked for a report.

Not the same road, friend. Matthew 2:12 says they “…withdrew to their country by another route.” After being warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they go home a different way. Same destination, different road.
